speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In gist, it is about fundamentally transforming the way the Home Team operates, in policing, emergency response, drug control, corrections and checkpoint security.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Home Team Transformation is an ambitious, multi-year plan requiring significant investments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our challenges are mounting and threats are evolving.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The work of the Home Team continues to rise in volume and complexity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A vibrant economy attracts more travellers and cargo moving through our checkpoints.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Cargo volumes went up by 25% over the same period.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Attacks are still happening around the world in the name of the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS), including those by self-radicalised lone wolves.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: While ISIS has suffered heavy territorial losses, its ideology continues to attract supporters, not least in our region.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Technological advancements have also brought about new security challenges.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: According to the United States (US) Center for Strategic and International Studies, the cost of cybercrime around the world may be as much as US$600 billion annually, or nearly 1% of global gross domestic product.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The new Home Team Science and Technology Agency will play a central role in ensuring that our investment achieves maximum operational impact.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It will be called "HTX" in short. "HT" stands for the Home Team while the "X" symbolises the agency's role as a Force Multiplier for the Home Team.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: First, HTX will build systems and solutions that will enhance the effectiveness and efficiency of the Home Team.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: One example is the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority's (ICA's) New Clearance Concept (NCC).

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have been used to large teams of officers manning rows of physical counters and clearing travellers manually.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: That will be a thing of the past.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: NCC imagines "breeze-through" clearance for citizens, who can walk through immigration channels without even taking out their passports.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Foreign visitors can perform self-clearance at automated immigration gates.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: NCC will bring about greater convenience to travellers, without compromising security.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: NCC will need to incorporate several different domains of technology which HTX will put together.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These include: a)	Biometrics solutions that will accurately capture a person’s biometric information.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The BioScreen-Multi Modal Biometrics System (MMBS), which takes iris, photo and fingerprint data, is one example. b)	Smart sensors, like cameras, can identify persons of interest, including those who have run afoul of the law. c)	Data science and artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms will be used to analyse advance information integrated from various sources, including the Electronic Arrival Card and advance passenger information from airlines.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The analysis will then be used to assess the risk profile of travellers before they arrive at our checkpoints.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Emergency response is another area that will be transformed through science and technology.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Data analytics can be used to dynamically identify where emergency resources should be deployed in advance, so that they can respond to the incidents faster when they occur.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: When an emergency call comes in, AI can be used to assist emergency call dispatchers in their work.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The system is able to not only recognise speech but also transcribe and log emergency calls.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: And when Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) officers respond to the incidents, robotics and unmanned systems can help to reduce their risk exposure and enhance safety.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: SCDF has already started to put on trial an exoskeleton which enables firefighters to carry heavy loads and improve their performance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Another example is the Pumper Firefighting Machine (PFM).

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is a firefighting robot that can be controlled remotely, and which has already been successfully deployed for operations at the frontline.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Besides science and technology capabilities, HTX will also strengthen our ability to procure and execute projects on time and on budget.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Thereafter, we must ensure that our capabilities are refreshed and updated to benefit from new advances.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Second, beyond systems and solutions, HTX will better enable the Home Team Departments (HTDs) to adopt a One Home Team approach, for example, in joint operations to respond to a terror incident.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: HTX will support the development of a Home Team Operations Centre.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will bring together all Operations Centres across the Home Team under one roof.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Enabled by technology, there can be faster communication and stronger coordination among responders from different HTDs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A common sense-making platform will allow HTDs to have a common situational picture, drawing feeds from Home Team officers responding to the incident, data from the island-wide sensors on the ground, media reports and so on.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A One Home Team approach will also extend to coordinating intelligence sharing and investigations across Home Team Departments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Having a single agency in the Home Team to develop systems and solutions will ensure coherent technical architecture and interoperability across our many systems.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will also enable greater synergies to be reaped.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In establishing HTX, scientific and technological resources across the Home Team will be consolidated within a single agency.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: By centralising our science and technology resources, there will be greater career progression and development opportunities for science and technology personnel.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: HTX will also recruit scientists and engineers for new positions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With the Home Team's increased demand for science and technology capabilities, HTX will need to grow its capacity in the coming years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will create exciting new Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) job opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: HTX will also add to the whole-of-Government push towards building up engineering expertise in the Public Service.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: By enhancing partnerships with counterparts, such as the Defence Science and Technology Agency (DSTA), Defence Science Organisation (DSO), Government Technology Agency (GovTech) and Health Sciences Authority (HSA), HTX will enrich the public service ecosystem of science and engineering talent.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Beyond the Public Service, HTX will be closely partnering industry and academia in its efforts to translate cutting-edge research into effective security solutions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These collaborations will serve to further boost the innovation ecosystem in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Having explained the mission and functions of HTX, I will now describe the significant elements of the Bill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Part 2 of the Bill establishes the functions and powers of the agency.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The functions are broadly aligned to HTX's mission as a force multiplier for the Home Team.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Adopting a whole-of-Government perspective, HTX will also be able to build new capabilities for other Government agencies that have similar technological needs as the Home Team departments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Parts 3 to 6 pertain to the formation of HTX’s Board, the decision-making procedures, personnel and financial matters.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These are similar to that of other major Statutory Boards and is consistent with the Public Sector Governance Act 2018.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Part 8 provides for the transfer of property, assets, liabilities and employees from the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) to HTX.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Chiefly, it includes an amendment to the First Schedule of the Criminal Law (Temporary Provisions) Act (CLTPA).

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The formation of this agency will not only build mission-critical capabilities within the Home Team, but create important synergies within the larger science and technology ecosystem in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In these ways, technology can help the Home Team work more effectively and efficiently, but the challenges continue.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The low total fertility rate, which was 1.16 last year, projects manpower shortage across different sectors.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Technology can be used to reduce the need for manpower.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, CNB is working on automating the process of registering and administering urine tests and using robots to handle the samples securely, reducing the need for manpower.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It streamlines the immigration process, allowing Singaporeans to experience a contactless immigration clearance as well as allowing first-time visitors to use automated immigration lanes.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This will help the ICA cope with increased travel while keeping the time needed to clear immigration low.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is especially important, given that the number of travellers transiting through and travelling to and from Singapore has increased drastically over the years.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Last year, there were 212 million travellers and this is projected to increase by 40% by 2025.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In order for Singapore to continue being a popular tourist destination and hub for international travel, it is important that the immigration clearance system be both fast and effective.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With increasing use of online shopping, the number of parcels being sent to and from other countries as well as within Singapore has increased exponentially.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Last year, there were 10 million consignments, containers and parcels.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is likely to increase by 70% by 2025.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In order to screen for illicit drugs, guns and other dangerous and prohibited items, it is important that the Home Team's capabilities are built up.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On 29 June this year, ICA detected 20 items suspected to be gun parts in a parcel marked "merchandise".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Although manpower coupled with machinery is a possible solution, the more sustainable and feasible way is through technology working in partnership with the excellent ICA officers and the Home Team officers that we have today.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Both their commitment, dedication, ability as people and officers, coupled with technology, I think that is the way for it, and that is exactly what we are wanting to do today.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Crime committed through the use of technology is increasing.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These included unauthorised access or transaction of online accounts, unauthorised purchase using credit or debit cards, and phishing emails.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Seventy percent of these e-commerce crimes happened on the popular e-commerce platform Carousell.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some of the unique challenges cybercrime pose to Police investigations around the world are the transnational nature of cybercrime, anonymity through Virtual Private Network or other anonymous proxy services, and availability of “cybercrime as a service” which allows less tech savvy persons to hire persons with high expertise knowledge and specialised tools and services to commit cybercrime on their behalf.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This shows that investing in science and technology to keep up with and outpace cybercriminals is necessary to ensure deterrence and rule of law in a world where an increasing number of transactions and communications are happening online.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Photos and videos can be doctored or fabricated almost indiscernibly.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Evidence can be fabricated and alibis can be falsified.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Fake news can be masqueraded as true and authoritative.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As deepfake technology speeds ahead, technology that detects deepfakes often plays catch-up.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, investment in forensic technology is necessary to keep up with technological advancements to prevent them from being used for malicious ends.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Atrocious child pornography syndicates and terror cells organise themselves online, making it harder to detect their activities.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While there is legislation that provides for powers to confiscate and access electronic devices, there will be situations where the Police will need to crack into the device without the password given to them.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Investment in technology and careful application of it are, therefore, important to administer justice, prevent recurrence and dismantle syndicates.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As terror attacks could be high tech, for example, through the use of commercial drones, or low tech, for example, through a vehicle-ramming incident or a knife attack, a wide variety of technology and science is needed to detect, prevent and counter terror attacks.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The factual matrix in any given attack situation is hardly ever the same.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While this agency is well-situated to solve the challenges and needs we see today, the agency would also ready our Home Team for the future.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: HTX will be at the forefront of technological and scientific developments.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some people say that criminals are two steps ahead and the authorities only play catch-up.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This agency that we are debating today, endeavours to prevent that situation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While it is grounded in the present, it also looks to the future.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By consolidating the Home Team’s related science and technology into a centralised location.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There can be deep collaboration over teams with overlapping science and technology expertise, overcoming the silo effect by bridging the space gap or the virtual space gap.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because iron sharpens iron, the galvanising environment will spur the individuals, officers and various groups working there to create even better ideas and possible solutions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There would be more opportunities for career progression even in the specialised area of science and technology.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This makes the career path longer term, allowing scientists and engineers to accumulate experience in the sensitivities of what the Home Team requires.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The career options can also be widened as there would be, quite possibly, more opportunities for transfers within the agency to related but different teams.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This would allow people to learn new skills, and apply old skills in new ways, while still utilising and increasing their experience in the Home Team.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Just as the career path is lengthened and widened, so also is the incentive for the Home Team to invest in and develop its scientists and engineers, further enabling Singapore to	benefit	from	cutting-edge	technology	in	its	home affairs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This could also incentivise students to read applied science and engineering which are important in an age of information and technology.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thirdly, it creates a centralised location where Home Team agencies can source for solutions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Instead of needing to hunt for research and technology partners with expertise in the area of research they are looking at for a solution, they are able to approach a single connecting point which will then be able to connect the most appropriate team to work on a solution to meet that need.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And it could be a very pressing need and time-sensitive.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Fourthly, having a dedicated agency for science and technology opens up greater collaboration opportunities with science and technology home departments in other countries.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It would be easier to explore and coordinate possible projects to collaborate on since all the Home Team-related science and technology teams are concentrated in a single agency.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The increased opportunity to work with counterparts in other countries and to learn from their experience will be valuable for the development of our Home Team capabilities and experiences.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even as this new Statutory Board allows science and technology to develop solutions for the Home Team’s unique challenges, what the Home Team needs is not always unrelated to what is needed by other agencies or Ministries.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, drone technology used for search and rescue could also be utilised by the Ministry of Defence (MINDEF) for reconnaisance operations or recce ops.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Will the Minister consider allowing for non-sensitive Home Team technology to be used in consumer products should the opportunity arise?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, if the Home Team develops video cameras that capture better quality images, these cameras can be used to enhance private security cameras and increase security throughout the island without necessarily installing a Police camera each and every time.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This would help strengthen the Home Team's ability to work with private security industry and private players to keep Singapore a safe country to live in and to respond quickly in the event of a crisis or terror attack.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It does so by utilising technology for their future and present challenges and by building up a strong team of technologists whose wealth of experience in the sensitivities of Home Team requirements will be able to help fashion future solutions fit for the Home Team’s purpose.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And for these reasons, Sir, I support the Bill.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Many welcomed the move to boost capabilities across the various security agencies, and said it was a timely move, given the continued global threats posed by terrorism as well as rising threats of cyberattacks and transnational crime.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Second Minister for Home Affairs Josephine Teo also highlighted during the debate that the greater use of science and technology will enable the Home Team to be effective, in the face of manpower constraints and future challenges.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Some made reference to the setting up of DSTA, a Statutory Board under MINDEF set up in 2000.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Dr Antonio L Rappa, an associate professor and head of Management and Security Studies at the Singapore University of Social Sciences' School of Business in an article in The Straits Times in February 2019 observed that the military sector has produced innovative variants for military security across the three branches of the Singapore Armed Forces.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: He said the Home Team, too, is quick to adopt new technologies.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: One example is the new body-cameras used by the Singapore Police Force (SPF).

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Also, officers involved in investigating crime can now access the most updated information anywhere in the region.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: SPF is also reportedly considering new infrared technology which has been used in a limited fashion for the Police Coast Guard units.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Second Minister Josephine Teo has also earlier given many exciting examples in her speech.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Dr Rappa also said that while Home Team officers do share some similarities with defence force officers, it is also clear that their different security functions and specialist nature of work require a different range of advanced technologies.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In Malay):   The proposal to set up a dedicated agency for the Home Team that can look into matters related science and technology is a good move.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: With our country facing a multitude of global challenges arising from terrorism, cyberattacks and transnational crimes, this agency will help to build the Home Team's capabilities to overcome increasingly complex issues.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The use of science and technology will also help the Home Team manage its manpower and meet new challenges.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: When this proposal was first announced, many made reference to DSTA which was established some time ago.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Through DSTA, the defence sector managed to come up with many innovative solutions for the three branches of the Singapore Armed Forces.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Home Team has also employed many new technologies.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The establishment of this dedicated agency will continue to strengthen such efforts and raise the capabilities of the security sector in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In English): I am, therefore, supportive of the setting up of the agency and this Bill.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I have a few quick comments and queries though.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The work of this agency will generate meaningful data and insights that may be useful to all departments within the Home Team and even other Government agencies.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The power of data and actionable insights being shared should not be underestimated.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There are also opportunities to collaborate with different agencies within the broader science and technology ecosystem to build a stronger and more meaningful science and technology sector for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There may also be existing partnerships which could be enhanced.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: On another note, as we use science and technology to improve surveillance and fight terrorism, there may be concerns of how privacy and personal data may be impacted.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It may also be useful to assure the public that any images, videos or data collected in the course of the use of various security innovations will be used in a proper manner and are well protected by a sound data security framework.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Notwithstanding my comments above, Mr Speaker, I stand in support of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Without doubt, the next decade holds the potential to surpass these changes at an even faster rate, with futuristic technological innovations becoming a reality.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Today, the Home Team faces increasing public expectations and scrutiny, changes in crime profile and increasing non-crime-related demand.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: They are expected to deliver improved services despite facing tough resource constraints.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: There is an ever-increasing pressure to deliver more, for less.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: With the addition of Digital Defence as the sixth pillar of Singapore's Total Defence strategy, the setting up of HTX to drive innovation and develop technologies to enhance the Home Team's capabilities is timely and much needed.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In my speech today, I would like to focus on two areas: (a) Evolving Operating Landscape; and (b) Predictive Policing.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The operating landscape for the Home Team has vastly evolved over the years, bringing about new challenges and expectations.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: We are witnessing the nature of crimes evolve with rapid advancement of technology.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Cyber-enabled crimes, in particular, are becoming more prevalent and sophisticated.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: False e-commerce transactions, fake loans and Internet love scams are now among the most common scams reported.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: How will the new agency work with existing ones, such as GovTech, the Ministry of Communications and Information and other Government agencies, to mitigate such breaches without duplicating existing efforts?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In the opening speech at the recent Interpol World 2019, Minister Josephine Teo highlighted three areas of innovation that hold promise – biometrics, data analytics and digital forensics.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, these areas of innovation have the potential to rapidly solve crime.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Biometrics facial recognition technology is able to scan through thousands of video footages to identify criminals.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Data analytics is able to plough through enormous amounts of data and improve sense-making.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Digital forensics has the ability to extract and analyse digital evidence from the latest Internet of Things (IOT) devices, among others.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: At the heart of the Home Team transformation, "digital" has to be about helping officers serve the public more effectively, enabling them to spend more time problem-solving, providing them the information required to make intelligent decisions faster, more effectively and in greater depth.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: And I would like to remind that the fundamental role of human instinct, emotional intelligence and pragmatic decision-making in responding to situations must be recognised in designing digital.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: My second point on predictive policing – declining birth-rates have led to an ageing population that will increase the demand for emergency services while at the same time putting constraints on the manpower available to the Home Team to tackle these challenges.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The Home Team needs to continuously innovate and leverage technology to fundamentally change the way it operates in order to deal with these challenges.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The most advanced crime analytics of the day relied on analysts leveraging on geographic information systems.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Regardless, the trends identified were based on what had happened and it did not provide any insight into where crime might shift.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The missing component was the ability to forecast where and when crime would occur or, in other terms, a transformation from retrospective to forecasting.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Predictive policing bridges those gaps by providing the best place and time for the Police to problem-solve.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: A driving force behind a shift in paradigms is the potential outcome for law enforcement to increase its effectiveness and efficiency, enhance criminal investigations, and to allow agencies to "work smarter".

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: It is within this political and social climate that predictive policing has emerged as a possibility of enhancing public safety.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Predictive policing can become a reality here in Singapore, similar to how predictive maintenance helps to avoid breakdowns of critical infrastructure in a way that is evidence-based, accountable and ethically sound, ultimately aiming to achieve crime reduction success, while functioning with fewer human resources and thereby reducing operating costs.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: There are several models of Predictive Policing that Singapore can learn from.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: One such model, the City Pulse project by the Dutch police, was highlighted by Second Minister Josephine Teo in her speech earlier.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: I would also urge our authorities to study the Vancouver Police Department's (VPD's) Predictive Policing Project that has yielded remarkable results.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The purpose of the evaluation was to determine whether police actions, guided by the forecasting system, would have a measurable impact on property crime, specifically residential break-and-enters.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Based on the positive crime reduction results and demonstrated ability to operationalise the technology in a police service, the predictive policing initiative was formalised and expanded into other areas of the organisation.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: One of the most innovative application being the Community Policing Block Watch Programme.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Block Watch is all about neighbours helping neighbours.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Participants watch out for one another’s homes and report suspicious activities to the police and one another.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The Block Watch Captains in each estate then electronically distribute a notification to their members, informing them of the increased risk with recommendations that they exercise increased vigilance during those times.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The community members are reminded not to directly engage with any suspicious individuals and to call the police emergency line should they witness any criminal or suspicious activities.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: This has the net effect of mobilising hundreds of citizens every day and providing actionable information to the community.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The ancillary benefit is that this process helps reinforce the connection and communication between the community and police that are often lacking in other Community Policing initiatives once they are formally established.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: This ongoing communication and feedback also help foster a more inclusive approach to crime prevention and one where the community plays a critical role in its success.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: It is from this pioneering use of predictive policing technology that the VPD accomplished what police services frequently struggled with, limited resources and the inability to reassign patrol officers from often a busy call-load and dedicated emergency response.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: This, I believe, is a worthwhile model from which Singapore can learn from and incorporate into SGSecure – a New Generation of Community Policing with Predictive Policing and Community Engagement.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Without deploying digital technology, the task of fighting crime and protecting citizens becomes almost impossibly tough in a world where citizens and criminals alike are increasingly digitally savvy.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Failure to adopt digital technologies also restricts the ability of our Home Team officers to operate effectively within an ever more constrained operating environment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The nature of modern threats to national security are increasingly complex and must be tackled through the use of cutting-edge science and technology.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That said, I have two points of clarifications to raise.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Section 11 of the Bill provides a list of four categories of individuals who are disqualified from serving as a member of this new Agency.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Indeed, in legislation that provides for the existence of other Statutory Boards, we see similar sections outlining these conditions for disqualification.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, this list is different from legislation providing for other Statutory Boards, such as the DSTA Act and the Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR) Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These two Statutory Boards either deal with similar science and technology topics or exist under the same category in the Public Sector (Governance) Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Speaking generally, the A*STAR Act bars those with mental illness, undischarged bankruptcy and unpardoned dishonest offences.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I raise two questions pertaining to this point.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Why are these conditions relevant here and why are they not relevant to the other Statutory Boards?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Two, does the Government have plans to harmonise these conditions of membership disqualification?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is about privacy, which fellow Member Rahayu Mahzam has raised as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Every Singapore Citizen appreciates the centrality of public safety and security to our way of life.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are able to walk on the streets at night with ease because we know that we will be safe.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, even as Singaporeans feel physically safe, they have also become uneasy at the risks involved with giving away their data.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A spate of data leakages from the Government has exacerbated such fears.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In its mission to keep Singapore safe, this new Agency will surely leverage heavy use of data.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second Minister Josephine Teo highlighted that the agency will make intensive usage of video analytics and surveillance in its crime deterrence and incident response.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have two specific recommendations to make on accountability mechanisms that can be implemented.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, will MHA publish annual reports on its data security measures to enhance public trust on this issue?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, will MHA consider setting up a hotline for employees to whistleblow on lax data security measures?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is paramount that the Government takes active steps to demonstrate transparency, accountability and security with the great powers our people have entrusted it with.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Take the example of the "smart lamp posts." ST Engineering won the tender last year and these lamps will hit the streets this year.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The press release has highlighted its benefits to society.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We will be able to better catch speeding motorists and personal mobility devices.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In times of a transport breakdown and traffic congestion, authorities can proactively provide solutions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But some citizens were also surprised by the extensiveness of its systems.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Because these street lamps will be able to identify faces in real time and because they might eventually be everywhere, this means that there is potentially no place in Singapore where you would not have data on your whereabouts stored in some Government database.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps, most Singaporeans will take the angle that if you do nothing wrong, you have no need to fear.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But if leaks of such pervasive, universal data ever happen, it could strongly undermine trust in our public institutions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the Ministry will take proactive steps to prevent such breaches from ever happening.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, like many other countries, we still face terrorist threats and other challenges from the evolving nature of crimes.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hence, it is necessary for us to utilise technology to enhance the capabilities of our Home Team.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, setting up a dedicated agency to gather expertise in science and technology to provide customised, dedicated solutions for the Home Team sounds very logical.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, in setting up this new agency, I would like to ask whether scarce research and development resources could be divided and diverted from current research and development (R&D) institutions.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I also want to express my concerns about the substantial budget allocated to this new agency and the accountability in the way funds are distributed and spent.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would appreciate it if the Ministry could share more details on how it justifies the amounts allocated and the measures to ensure accountability and transparency in its spending.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My second clarification concerns this – that the new organisation will focus on areas critical to the Home Team's operations, namely, sense-making and surveillance, forensics, robotics and unmanned systems.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Could more be done in this area of research to defend us against the threat of bioterrorism or biological attacks?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I commend the bringing together of more than 1,000 research scientists, engineers and technical staff from the Home Team departments in the setting up of the new agency to focus on developing cutting-edge technologies, such as detection and surveillance capability, forensics as well as robotics and unmanned systems, to safeguard Singapore in this digital age.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: However, as we continue to amass the latest and increasingly sophisticated technologies in surveillance and data analytics in our homeland security arsenal, I would like to take this opportunity to highlight three areas of concern for this House and the Ministry to consider.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: First, we must ask ourselves what is the impact on the society's prevailing mindset and mental health as we live under the constant gaze of surveillance with security technologies becoming more chillingly ubiquitous.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Second, as we increase the use of AI and surveillance in a preventive manner, whether for criminal actions or terrorist threats, what are the implications of algorithmic biases and unwarranted systemic discrimination on our multiracial and multicultural society?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: How do we maintain a resilient and cohesive society with unbiased policing as we fight terrorism with new technologies?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, how are we creating a culture of respect for privacy and accountability as the presence of numerous surveillance and data analytic methods by Government agencies makes it difficult for individuals to control the use of their data?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Technologies that allow the Government to monitor, analyse and manage behaviour to fight crime, detect threats and keep us safe are also the same technologies that may paradoxically give us less psychological safety and have detrimental consequences on our society’s mental well-being.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We already have an existing and extensive network of security cameras but the use of more sophisticated technologies on these cameras means information could be shared among agencies.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: According to a report by The Straits Times, the new camera systems can, for instance, analyse faces – down to race, gender and age – for catching speeding e-scooter riders and other purposes.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: With the surveillance information, Government agencies can increase their situational awareness, detect potential problems and respond quickly to incidents, such as unruly crowds, train breakdowns and traffic congestion.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It has been shown that the fear and uncertainty generated by surveillance inhibit activity more than any action by the Police.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This is clearly a good outcome for law and order.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, Mr Speaker, we must not forget that the well-being of our citizens goes beyond just physical safety and security.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This constant state of being monitored shapes an environment where one’s sense of personal control becomes greatly diminished.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We behave in a desired way just in case we are being watched.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Another research by Duke University from 1966, which has been cited in numerous other articles and books on privacy even to today, showed that the shrinkage of free space where a person can be "off-stage" and simply be themselves rather than trying to be respectable under society's standards may increase the frequency of anxiety and withdrawal from social roles, which are signs of mental illness.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Other studies have also argued and reported that the long-term damage on one's psyche from prolonged surveillance creates a culture of self-censorship and apprehension which clearly inhibits creativity and innovation, the very bedrock for the future of our economy and our Smart Nation vision.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Unless the mental well-being of our citizens is the top priority in policy narratives, we may never intentionally and adequately address the tradeoffs between the security imperative and potentially suffocating psychological effects of living under the gaze of the authority.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Again, let me use this example of the 100,000 Police Cameras (PolCams).

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: How did we decide how much surveillance is enough when we currently already have a desirable low crime rate?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: While predictive policing through AI is the future of data-driven law enforcement because of convenience and accuracy in the face of potential threats, we cannot ignore the risks that may arise with unwarranted systemic biases that might lead to inadvertent discrimination towards some communities.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Predictive policing risks reinforcing known biases in law enforcement.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Bias may also lead to the over-policing of certain communities, heightening tensions, or, conversely, the under-policing of communities that may actually need law enforcement intervention but do not feel comfortable in alerting the Police.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: These neural networks are built on a vast number of faces from different groups.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As a result, if it is trained and built for the better part on male subjects from the ethnic majority, for example, which is statistically more likely, the system will be more accurate for this group and less accurate for others.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This raises concerns that face surveillance used by governments can fuel discriminatory surveillance and target racial minorities.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This is worrying, as suspicion can be activated based on culture, religion and ethnicity as legitimate identifiers of threat.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore’s multicultural context, inadvertent algorithmic bias can put our harmonious social fabric at risk.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: No community must be perceived to be singled out.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Second Minister please clarify the safeguards and mitigating measures we have in place to avoid such misidentifications and algorithmic biases?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Last but not least, Mr Speaker, please let me share my third concern on data privacy and accountability.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: An article by TODAY in 2016 claimed that Singaporeans saw national security as more important than privacy.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Nevertheless, this does not offset the value of privacy and the need for the Government to remain accountable to its citizens.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Convenience cannot be the sole consideration of data collection.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Citizens deserve to know the purpose and how their data is being used.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, if we want to create a culture of respect for privacy, the way the Government handles individuals’ data must set the example.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: While the Government has in place the Public Sector (Governance) Act where Government agencies can share relevant data only when there are data sharing directions issued by relevant Ministers, citizens may not be aware of what these directions entail and how their data is being shared among agencies.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: When the public is aware of the efforts that the Government takes to safeguard their data, trust with the Government is built and the public live in less fear that their every action is subject to scrutiny.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: With transparent safeguards, the public also play the role of a compliance officer, as they can identify lapses that occur.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, I urge the Government to consider informing the public on what kinds of data different Government agencies are authorised to access and use and for what purposes, to build a more informed citizenry.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Public Sector Data Security Review Committee had identified technical, process and people strategies to strengthen our data security regime, given the rising complexity of our systems as our demand to use data grows in our society.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It has found that there are varying levels of training on data protection in the public sector and that many data incidents have previously been the result of human error.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, it is not just the Government systems that are at risk but also the ecosystem with which our citizens' data interacts with.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In the meantime, I would like to urge the Government to consider constituting an independent oversight body that will evaluate, on an annual basis, whether various forms of personal data, collected through forms or surveillance, has been legally and properly collected and managed by the public officers.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This would include reviewing cases of misuse, the public organisation's data management culture and whether any changes have to be made to prevent future cases of misuse or breaches.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In the United Kingdom, the Investigatory Powers Commissioner's Office (IPCO) provides independent oversight of the use of investigatory powers by intelligence agencies, police forces and other public authorities.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: IPCO is comprised of judicial personnel, scientific experts, inspectors, lawyers and communications experts.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In the US, the US Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board reviews information-sharing practices related to terrorism protection efforts.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Establishing an oversight body is important as the Government increasingly gathers massive amounts of information with new surveillance measures, including smart lamp-posts and drone cameras, being rolled out.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The report of this body should be made public to ensure state accountability and to also demonstrate the respect that the Government has on data privacy.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It is tempting to brush off the concerns shared above with the rhetoric of "it's better to be safe than sorry" or "if you have nothing to hide, it won't affect you".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: However, we must ask ourselves what is the kind of society we want Singapore to become.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The agency will enable the Home Team to stay in the forefront of science and innovation, with the mission to develop the best capabilities to address national security threats now and, more importantly, in the future.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Core to the success of this new agency will be the strategy and ability of the agency to attract and develop a world-class team with STEM and digital skills.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Without strong science and technology capability, the Agency will not be able to deliver its mission for the Home Team.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With digital transformation on the agenda for many businesses and Singapore's drive to building a Smart Nation, there is a high demand for skilled STEM and digital talent.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Roles in high demand across all industries and the public sector are data scientists, user experience designers and digital roles.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Cybersecurity, of course, continues to be an area of focus.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, with the competing demands on a limited talent pool, the ability to attract and retain good talent will be critical for the agency.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The agency's people strategy to centralise recruitment, development and management of all Science and Technology personnel across the Home Team is sound.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It will also need to have a strategy to build a pipeline of STEM and digital talent.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But while the focus of this talent pool will be deep skills in science and technology, it is important to keep in mind that innovation will require more than that.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Innovation requires technology, but it also requires human insights and the willingness to think and to see things differently.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And to this point, the Minister's elaboration on the agency's One Home Team approach is welcomed.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And I think the points made by other Members with regard to the privacy concerns and how technology will be used, these are all very critical in pointing out that while we are focusing on an agency that looks at Science and Technology and the deployment of technology, what is important is the actual usage and how it is implemented.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And, in doing that, I think the human side of things, the insights, will be very critical and, of course, the policies behind them.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Faced with the rapid pace of change and against a landscape of evolving crimes, increasing terrorist and security threats, and the pace of change, I do agree that the Home Team does need to have its own capabilities to be able to ensure preparedness, combat crime and keep Singapore safe.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While the Home Team builds its own capabilities, we must ensure that the efforts are coordinated throughout the whole of Government to minimise duplication and, more importantly, that research and development are effective.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will ensure that the agency, together with the whole of Government, keeps pace and develops the best capabilities for crime prevention as well as to protect Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Apart from the organisations that MHA has partnered, even within the public sector, there are other agencies focused on similar areas that the new HTX has outlined for itself.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These include the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore (CSA) as well as the Smart Nation and Digital Government Group.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Using and deploying technology securely and the better use of the vast amounts of data for insights to serve our citizens more effectively are clearly priorities for all Government agencies.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While I agree that the Home Team does have its unique requirements and requires deep capabilities to be able to meet these needs, there are also many areas of similarities with what the other agencies and industry are working on, for example, data science and analytics, cybersecurity and AI.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The difference is in the application of the technology or solutioning and domain knowledge.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Home Team is not alone in the quest to build science and technology capabilities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The ability to work together across the agencies and industry will allow leverage and enable the realising of the value of synergies across the larger science and technology ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These coordination and partnership are also key when we look in the area of talent and skills, given the limited talent pool of STEM capability and digital skills in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As we build new capabilities for the future, it is important to balance technology with operational needs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While technical talent is key for innovation, it is equally important that the operational talent within the agencies is also tech-savvy.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The reason for this is to allow for operational and technology integration so that operational and technology talent can have a common language for more effective outcomes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This combination of operational insights and new capabilities can lead to the discovery of new ways to seeing and doing things and for more effective execution and delivery of services.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The best way to do that is really to work together to look at the implementation in the operational context so that people can understand the value beyond just the convenience of the use of technology.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This brings to mind some examples when we always say, "Do not collect information" because if you do not store it and you do not keep it well, it is a concern.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But when you need that information, you really wish you had collected it because you cannot turn back the clock.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And this is the same with regard to technology.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Looking at the areas of work and terms of reference of HTX, I see possible overlap of work and duplication with the science and technology agencies already in existence, such as DSTA, MINDEF, GovTech, HSA, DSO and A*STAR.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Some of these capabilities and expertise already reside within these agencies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: What then is the rationale for setting up an HTX and not tapping on expertise residing within an existing Ministry or agency like MINDEF, DSTA or DSO?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Whether it is systems engineers, specialists in marine and maritime engineering, technology or logistics specialists or even specialist forensic investigation, these experts are already serving in these agencies safeguarding Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Should we not strengthen those existing agencies, instead of having to set up another dedicated agency?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Notwithstanding, if HTX is eventually set up, how is the agency going to not just value add but value create for the Home Team and Singapore in terms of safety and security?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Singapore has a tight labour market situation and there are exacting manpower needs and a demand for talent, such as engineers and so on.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Every additional new headcount created will be a strain for those hiring outside of the public sector.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With the setting up of HTX, I have some burning questions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: How many are fresh hires outside of the Home Team and public sector?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: How many are transferred from each of the Home Team units, such as SCDF, SPF, MHA Headquarters, ICA, Prisons and so on?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Will there be personnel transferred from outside the Home Team, such as DSTA, DSO, HSA and GovTech?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: For those within the Home Team or related Government agencies and are transferred to HTX, I am deeply concerned about their interests, welfare and their fate, including career progression and terms and conditions of service.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I am aware the Bill states in explicit terms that they will not be worse off.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I think the question is not just whether they will be worse off at the point when they are transferred over, but more in terms of their long-term prospects and future.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is especially pertinent as many of them may be in different schemes of service, such as the Pension scheme, Invest scheme or other similar schemes of service, which are unique to their service.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: These officers who may be affected by the transfer would naturally be concerned and uncertain about their future and what lies ahead.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Section 47(5) of the Bill states that the employee being transferred will be on existing terms until such time the conditions of employment are drawn up by the agency.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Similarly, as with the setting up of any new agency, amalgamation or integration, there will be new cultures to adapt to and new management to adjust to.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Can the Minister assure this House that the affected employees will be well taken care of and truly be no worse off in the short term as well as in the long term?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This simply means employees employed in HTX may go on strike, but they are guilty of an offence if notice of intention to strike is not given to their employers at least 14 days before the strike.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I appreciate the sensitive nature of the work of HTX and that we must not and cannot afford strikes and disruption in such a sensitive area.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Naturally, some are concerned as to whether it is something that infringes the right of every worker in Singapore and whether we are compromising the rights of workers in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As employees of a Statutory Board, I assume that they can be union members and form a trade union and be collectively and individually represented.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I look forward to HTX working out an arrangement, together with the trade union movement, to ensure that workers within HTX are represented and adequately protected.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There is, however, explicit mention of the Minister and the agency members and I hope they will be able to exercise their powers judiciously and effectively for the safety and security of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Many Members spoke at length about why it is important for MHA to leverage science and technology to address the challenges ahead and to set up the new HTX.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As Members have rightly pointed out, the growth of new technologies has changed the Home Team's operating environment.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: New threats are emerging as our adversaries are also taking advantage of technological advances.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Home Team must, therefore, not be handicapped on this front.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will need to invest in building new capabilities and transform the way we work.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The setting up of a dedicated HTX is to achieve these purposes effectively and efficiently.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Mohamed Irshad asked about the capabilities that HTX will build.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, HTX scientists will conduct leading-edge research into the forensic analysis of suspected drug compounds.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Advances in DNA forensics will boost the Police's capability to generate leads for criminal investigations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Digital forensics and tackling cybercrime are another area of focus for HTX.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu asked about countering biological threats.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The detection and handling of chemical, biological or radiological materials are an important area for HTX.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: HTX will work with SCDF and related agencies, such as the National Environment Agency, to develop sensor systems to detect such materials and the capability to effectively respond to incidents involving hazardous materials.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These unique capabilities demonstrate why MHA is setting up HTX instead of leveraging other existing agencies like DSTA, DSO or GovTech.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is also Dr Chia Shi-Lu's question as well as Mr Patrick Tay's.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The mission, operating environment and requirements of these agencies are different from those of the Home Team.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Technological solutions and applications need to be customised or, in some cases, built organically.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is a point that Ms Jessica Tan emphasised.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There is enough scale within the Home Team to merit a dedicated science and technology agency, give specific focus on areas that would otherwise remain ancillary.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If you do not put it as the focus of a particular dedicated agency, then you must run the risk that these are ancillary to other agencies.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Whether you can build up sufficient capabilities in a short time to counter the challenges, that would be a question mark.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think that is an important point to make because if we were not to be able to plug the gaps that we identify, it actually is a disservice to Singaporeans, who obviously expect us to be up to speed, up to mark in all of these areas that we face threats in.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But I must stress that the agencies, even though they are dedicated and separate, they do not operate in silos.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They do cooperate very closely with one another and, later on, I will also give some examples.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked who HTX will be accountable to.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As such, the Minister for Home Affairs has overall responsibility for the agency.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Minister is, in turn, accountable to the Cabinet and to Parliament.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And to Dr Chia Shi-Lu's specific question about accountability for budgeting as well as utilisation, the same Parliamentary and audit processes that apply to all Government Statutory Boards will apply to HTX as well.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I recall when I was in Ministry of Finance, for example, the Estimates Committee, which consists of Members of Parliament, posed tough questions on Ministries' utilisation of the Budget.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: HTX will be subjected to the same discipline.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Patrick Tay also asked about the classification of HTX services as an essential service under the CLTPA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is the same as services provided by the Home Team, which are also deemed as essential services.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: HTX employees are, however, not Home Affairs Uniform Scheme officers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They will, therefore, be allowed to join the unions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked about the transfer of employees to the new HTX scheme.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Patrick Tay also raised important questions about career prospects as well as how we get the different cultures to work together.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is a Home Team culture, to begin with.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But the short answer to Mr Patrick Tay's question on career prospects is that it is certainly in HTX's own interest to ensure that officers feel motivated and want to give of their best.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, I see no reason why HTX leadership would want to slacken on this front.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Louis Ng had a question about clause 11 of the Bill which lists the five categories of individuals who are disqualified from serving on HTX's Board, and why these are different from that of A*STAR and DSTA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The categories listed are the same as Statutory Boards that were set up in recent years.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This includes GovTech and the Info-communications Media Development Authority, which are both agencies in the technology domain.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Statutory Boards adopt these categories as a measure of good governance.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As for his suggestion to standardise this across all Statutory Boards, we will refer this to the Public Service Division for their consideration.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Lastly, Dr Chia Shi-Lu had a question on funding for HTX.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: HTX, like other Statutory Boards, will submit its annual report and accounts to Parliament.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Specifically, they have queries and suggestions on the collection, sharing and security of data, all of which are very important.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The collection of data will continue to be done by the respective Home Team Departments, in accordance with their statutory duties or to maintain their mission effectiveness.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: That is something they will have to continue doing.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, ICA is required by the National Registration Act to collect personal information from residents.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Police Officers may also ask for a person's particulars as part of a criminal investigation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is unlikely that HTX officers will collect any kind of personal data in the course of their duties.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: HTX will, however, play the important role of safeguarding the Home Team's information technology (IT) systems and the data they hold.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Operating 24/7, M.SOC will proactively monitor and detect suspicious activities or attempted intrusions into the MHA network.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: M.SOC will also provide immediate response and investigate into cybersecurity incidents and issues.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: While we continue to improve data security protocols, the sharing of data among public agencies must also carry on.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As Ms Rahayu Mahzam has pointed out, data and insight sharing across Government agencies can lead to better outcomes for citizens.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: One such example is how Traffic Police shares accident data with the Land Transport Authority (LTA).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This helps LTA identify junctions or roads for engineering redesign and enhancements to improve road safety.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Anthea Ong and Mr Mohamed Irshad also raised concerns about privacy as we improve our surveillance capability.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think Ms Anthea Ong talked about the stress related to increased surveillance.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I believe Members of this House, being all public figures, can relate to that kind of stress.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We are very conscious of the need to protect privacy.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In this regard, we have strict protocols in place to ensure that only officers with proper authorisation can access them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The feedback we have received about PolCam is that the public feel safer with the cameras.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And indeed, in tandem with other Police enforcement efforts, PolCam has resulted in the sharp reduction of many crimes, such as property crimes and unlicensed moneylending harassment.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: PolCam footages have also been critical in solving many crimes and locating missing persons.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: MHA takes its responsibility as a custodian of the data it collects very seriously and will continue to pay careful attention to this.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will also work closely with GovTech and CSA to ensure a whole-of-Government approach to data and cybersecurity.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: MHA is currently working together with other Government agencies to review our data security policies and practices as part of the review process under the Public Sector Data Security Review Committee led by Senior Minister Teo Chee Hean.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Committee takes the key guiding principle that the Government places utmost importance on its duty to use citizens' data responsibly and securely.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, responsibility and security are the key guiding principles for the Committee.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is very much in line with the spirit of Members' suggestions on how MHA can protect citizens' data better.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I am sure that the Committee will also take into consideration Members' specific concerns and suggestions, and we will certainly raise them in our discussions with the Committee.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If I may paraphrase Ms Jessica Tan, we must also, at the same time as being cautious, not become paralysed by fear.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If we do not try to use data responsibly and securely, for good purposes, then we will also never learn, and that would be a missed opportunity.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Jessica Tan spoke about HTX's future success being contingent on its ability to attract and develop science and technology talent.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The key determinant of HTX's success will be the quality of its people.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: That is why HTX will have a two-fold human resources strategy.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Patrick Tay has asked about the establishment.
